"Temporarily" means: for a limited period of time — not permanently, not forever.

When something happens temporarily, it has a built-in end. It will stop, change, or go back to how it was before. The current state is not the final state.

That's the whole idea in one sentence: it won't last.
What the Word Silently Tells You

Every time you use "temporarily," you're actually communicating three things at once, even without saying them:

  1. The situation is not permanent. There's an expiry on it, even if no one knows exactly when.
  2. A change is expected. Either things will return to normal, or something new will follow.
  3. The duration is unspecified. "Temporarily" does not tell you how long — only that it's limited. It could be minutes, days, months, or even years, as long as there's an understanding that it will end.

This third point surprises many learners. "Temporarily" is not the same as "briefly." Something can be temporary and yet last a long time — a temporary job could run for two years. The word is about limitation, not shortness.
How It Works in a Sentence

"Temporarily" is an adverb. Its job is to describe or qualify a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It answers the question: "For how long?"

It can sit before the word it modifies, or after:

The road is temporarily closed.
The road is closed temporarily.

Both are correct. The first (before the verb/adjective) is slightly more formal and direct.
Examples Across Different Situations

Let's look at "temporarily" at work in real sentences. Notice how in every case, the word signals that the current state is not final:

  • The website is temporarily unavailable.

(It's down right now, but it'll come back.)

  • She is temporarily living with her parents.

(She's there for now, but it won't be forever.)

  • He temporarily forgot his password.

(He couldn't remember it in that moment, but then he did.)

  • The company temporarily halted production.

(They stopped for now, but plan to resume.)

  • The school is temporarily being used as a flood shelter.

(It's serving a different purpose right now — but it will return to being a school.)

  • He temporarily lost his balance.

(He stumbled for a second, then steadied himself.)

  • The CEO is temporarily stepping down due to health reasons.

(She may return to the role later.)
The Clearest Way to Understand It: The Contrast

The sharpest way to grasp "temporarily" is to place it next to its direct opposite: permanently.

The bridge is temporarily closed. → It will reopen.
The bridge is permanently closed. → It will never reopen.

She temporarily left the city. → She came back (or plans to).
She permanently left the city. → She's never coming back.

This is a temporary fix. → Someone will do a proper repair later.
This is a permanent fix. → It's done and settled.

The rule: "temporarily" = an end is coming. "permanently" = no end is coming.
How Long Is "Temporarily"?

This is important: the word gives you no specific duration. You need context for that.

  • He temporarily lost consciousness. → Probably seconds or minutes.
  • The office is temporarily closed. → Probably days or weeks.
  • She temporarily moved abroad for work. → Could be months or years.
  • The ancient Romans temporarily occupied that region. → Decades, in historical writing.

In every case, the speaker or writer knows — or believes — that the state will not last. How long it lasts depends entirely on the situation, not on the word itself.
Comparison with Similar Words

Several words feel close to "temporarily." Here's how to tell them apart:

Briefly
Means for a short time, with emphasis on shortness. "Temporarily" only says the time is limited — not that it was short.

He briefly paused. (a short pause)
He temporarily paused. (a limited pause — could be short or long, but it ended)

For now
Means at this present moment, subject to change. It's more casual and conversational. "Temporarily" is slightly more formal and more explicit about the limited nature.

I'm staying here for now. (casual)
I'm staying here temporarily. (clearer and slightly more formal)

For the time being
Almost identical in meaning to "temporarily." It means during this current period, but not permanently. You can usually swap them freely.

For the time being, the manager is away. = The manager is temporarily away.

Provisionally
Means as a temporary arrangement that may become permanent, depending on what happens — it has a "trial period" feeling to it.

He was provisionally appointed. (might become permanent based on performance)
He was temporarily appointed. (definitely a placeholder, not intended to be permanent)
The Tone It Carries

Here's something subtle but important: "temporarily" often acts as a softener when something negative is happening. It signals: don't worry, this will pass.

Compare these pairs:

The power is out. (just a fact — no comfort offered)
The power is temporarily out. (it'll come back — don't panic)

The app is down. (a plain statement)
The app is temporarily down. (a reassurance: it will work again)

This is why you see "temporarily" so often in official notices, customer service messages, and announcements. It's doing two jobs at once: reporting the current state and reassuring you that it isn't forever.

The flip side is also true — "temporarily" can deflate something positive:

He is the manager. (sounds settled and certain)
He is temporarily the manager. (he might not hold it long — don't get too attached)
Where You'll Commonly See It

"Temporarily" appears most often in:

  • Technical/service notices: This feature is temporarily unavailable.
  • Construction/repairs: The road is temporarily closed for resurfacing.
  • Medical contexts: She was temporarily blinded by the flash of light.
  • Work/life transitions: He's temporarily based in Mumbai.
  • Official/legal language: The law is temporarily suspended.
  • Emergency situations: Residents were temporarily evacuated from the area.
A Note on the Adjective Form

Since you're learning the adverb "temporarily," it helps to know its parent word: the adjective "temporary."

  • Temporary (adjective) = describes a noun as being non-permanent.
    A temporary job. A temporary fix. A temporary home.*
  • Temporarily (adverb) = describes how a verb or adjective applies — specifically, that it applies for a limited time only.
    She temporarily works here. The road is temporarily closed.*

The adverb form is simply the adjective at work inside a sentence to modify actions and states rather than nouns.
What Not to Get Wrong

1. Don't say "temporarily" when something is actually permanent.
Saying "The shop is temporarily closed" when it has shut down forever is misleading — either to comfort people falsely or by accident. The word carries a promise of change.

2. Don't assume "temporarily" means "briefly."
A temporary arrangement can be long-lasting. "She temporarily moved to London" could mean she was there for three years — but she always planned to come back.

3. Don't assume you know the duration from the word alone.
"Temporarily" gives you no time information. All it tells you is: this will not go on forever. For how long — you need the rest of the sentence or the situation to tell you.
Summary

"Temporarily" = for a limited time, not permanently.

It tells you: the current situation has an end. Something will change — either a return to how things were before, or a move to something new. It does not tell you how long the period is. It often softens bad news by hinting that things will improve. Its opposite is permanently. Its closest synonyms are for the time being and for now, though it is slightly more formal than both.
